subject: Family, Religion and Moral Education (FAREME)
curriculum: Zimbabwe Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (MoPSE) - Junior (Grade 3-7)
syllabus_source: Family, Religion and Moral Education Junior School Level Teacher's Guide, Grade 3-7, 2015-2022 - official MoPSE document, fetched and verified directly
confidence_flag: This file is grounded directly in the official FAREME Junior Teacher's Guide, retrieved in full. The complete list of Grade 3-7 topics/sub-topics (Family, Religion, Morals and Values, Religion and Health) is verified/exact from the source, as is the Religion topic's Grade 3-7 scope-and-sequence progression and a worked example of breaking the Family topic into teachable units. The source gives worked examples at specific grades (e.g. Family structure/names/totems/resources, Indigenous Religion at Grade 4) rather than a complete grade-by-grade table for every sub-topic, so grade placement for sub-topics beyond Religion should be treated as indicative rather than a fully verified per-grade chart.

chunks.content: FAREME is a Junior School humanities learning area designed to promote learners' awareness and appreciation of different religions practised in Zimbabwe. It seeks to develop family cohesion, unity, moral uprightness, inclusivity and tolerance, grounded in Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu values. The syllabus takes a multi-faith, non-proselytising and non-confessional, learner-centred, hands-on, problem-posing approach - meaning it teaches learners *about* different religions (Indigenous Religion, Christianity, Judaism, Islam) rather than promoting any single faith, helping learners reflect on their lives in a socio-religious context and develop religious tolerance.

chunks.topic: The 4 Main Topics and Their Sub-Topics
chunks.content: The Grade 3-7 FAREME syllabus is organised into 4 main topics: (1) Family - covering Concept of Family, Family and religion, Family and community, and Social and Emotional Learning; (2) Religion - covering Concept of religion, Indigenous religion, Christianity, Judaism, and Islam; (3) Morals and Values - covering the concept of morals and values, rights and responsibilities, conflict and conflict management, national value systems, and religion's relationship to technology and enterprise; (4) Religion and Health - covering religion and abuse, religion and gender, religion and sexuality, religion/HIV/AIDS, and healthy living.

Cross-cutting themes relevant to FAREME include: gender roles and equity in religion, enterprise skills, collaboration, sexuality/HIV/AIDS, guidance and counselling, heritage studies, the Constitution of Zimbabwe, children's rights and responsibilities, environmental issues, and disaster risk management. Time allocation is 4 periods of 30 minutes per week for Grade 3-7. Assessment is 30% continuous assessment and 70% summative assessment across all Junior grades.

chunks.topic: Religion - Verified Grade 3-7 Scope and Sequence
chunks.content: The official scope-and-sequence for the Concept of Religion sub-topic progresses as: Grade 3 - Religion in the family; Grade 4 - Religion in the community; Grade 5 - Religion in the country; Grade 6 - Religion in Africa; Grade 7 - Religions of the World. This shows the syllabus's spiral approach in action: the same core concept (religion) is revisited every year, but the scope widens outward each grade - from the learner's own family, to their community, to their country, to the African continent, and finally to a global view by Grade 7.

chunks.topic: Indigenous Religion - Teachable Units (Grade 4 Worked Example)
chunks.content: The syllabus guide gives Indigenous Religion at Grade 4 as a worked example of breaking a broad topic into teachable units. The core concepts to cover are: Historical Background, Roles of ancestors, Songs and dances, Religious practitioners, Key teachings, Food laws, and Taboos. These can be broken down even further into smaller lesson units, e.g. Indigenous Religion can be split into: Origin of Indigenous Religion, Roles of ancestors, and Family ancestors - each becoming its own timed, resourced lesson.
learning_activities: Discussing the origins of Indigenous Religion (where and when)
Researching the roles of ancestors within the family

chunks.topic: Family Structure, Names/Totems, and Resources - Worked Teachable Units
chunks.content: Under the Family topic, the guide gives worked examples of teachable units: 'Structure of the family' (learners describe and compare/contrast family structures - nuclear, monogamous, polygamous, child-headed, one-parent families), 'Family names and totems' (learners identify family names/members and state family totems, connecting to Heritage Studies content on totems), and 'Family Resources' (learners identify and list family possessions). Each unit is designed to build critical thinking, technology and innovation, problem solving, and decision-making competencies.
learning_activities: Discussing different family structures: nuclear, monogamous, polygamous, child-headed, one-parent
Researching and discussing family names and totems

chunks.topic: Right and Wrong - Worked Lesson Example (Grade 5)
chunks.content: The guide's worked lesson plan example for Morals and Values (Grade 5) has learners distinguish right from wrong and explain right and wrong in human behaviour, assuming learners already have some prior knowledge about morals and values from their families. The lesson has learners cite good morals and values found across different religions, then discuss in groups what various religions teach about morals and values, before reporting back their findings to the class.
learning_activities: Citing good morals and values in different religions
Group discussion on what various religions say about morals and values
Reporting back findings to the class

chunks.content: The Morals and Values topic covers: the concept of morals and values, rights and responsibilities, conflict and conflict management, national value systems, and religion's relationship to technology and enterprise. This topic connects religious teaching directly to practical everyday ethics and citizenship, including modern themes like how religious/moral values apply to technology use and enterprise/business conduct.

The Religion and Health topic covers: religion and abuse, religion and gender, religion and sexuality, religion/HIV/AIDS, and healthy living. This topic connects religious and moral teaching to sensitive but important life-skills areas, addressed through the syllabus's cross-cutting themes on sexuality/HIV/AIDS education and guidance and counselling, always via the syllabus's inclusive, non-confessional, multi-faith approach rather than any single religious viewpoint.

Suggested methods for teaching FAREME include: lesson delivery and note-taking, discussion, drama, role-play and simulation, video and film shows, e-learning, group work, research, case studies, and educational tours. Methods should minimise rote learning and instead promote curriculum competencies, supported by multi-sensory approaches (individualisation, totality, concreteness, self-activity, tactility and wholeness) to address learners' residual senses and keep the learner at the centre of the process.
